_note: Approximate USDA 2023 hardiness-zone ranges and typical frost windows for the populated parts of each state. Frost dates vary by elevation and microclimate; every page tells the reader to confirm their own date with their county extension office. Sources linked on each page: USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map (planthardiness.ars.usda.gov) and the state's land-grant extension service.

states.name: Alabama
states.note: Long warm season; fall is the best time for the cool-season five.

states.name: Alaska
states.last_frost: late May to mid-June (Anchorage and Fairbanks)
states.note: Short season with very long days; start warm-season crops indoors and grow them under cover.

states.name: Arizona
states.first_frost: late November to early December in the low desert; late September in the high country
states.note: Low-desert gardeners sow cool-season crops from October to February and avoid midsummer.

states.name: Arkansas
states.note: Two full cool seasons a year, spring and fall.

states.name: California
states.last_frost: frost-free on much of the coast; mid-March in the Central Valley; May in the mountains
states.first_frost: none on the coast; mid-November in the Central Valley
states.note: Coastal gardens grow the cool-season five nearly year round.

states.name: Colorado
states.note: High altitude means cold nights; use row cover for warm-season transplants.

states.name: Connecticut
states.note: Classic four-season garden; start tomatoes, peppers and eggplant indoors in March.

states.name: Delaware
states.note: Mild, humid summers suit cucumbers and melons.

states.name: Florida
states.last_frost: mid-February in the north; frost-free in the south
states.first_frost: December in the north; none in the south
states.note: The main vegetable season runs fall through spring; summer heat is the off season.

states.name: Georgia
states.note: Fall plantings of kale, spinach, carrots and beets often beat spring ones.

states.name: Hawaii
states.note: Sow year round; choose the cooler, drier months for spinach and kale.

states.name: Idaho
states.last_frost: early May (Boise) to early June (eastern Idaho)
states.note: Cool nights and dry air; melons need the warmest spot in the garden.

states.name: Illinois
states.note: Rich soils and hot summers; tomatoes and peppers thrive.

states.name: Indiana
states.note: Direct sow the cool-season five in early April and again in early August.

states.name: Iowa
states.note: Deep prairie soil; carrots and beets size up well.

states.name: Kansas
states.note: Hot, windy summers; mulch and water deeply.

states.name: Kentucky
states.note: Long enough season for two rounds of every cool-season crop.

states.name: Louisiana
states.note: Fall and winter are prime time for spinach, kale, carrots, beets and turnips.

states.name: Maine
states.note: Short season; start every warm-season crop indoors and choose the sunniest bed.

states.name: Maryland
states.note: Humid summers; give cucumbers and melons airflow and a trellis.

states.name: Massachusetts
states.last_frost: late April (Cape Cod) to late May (Berkshires)
states.note: Start tomatoes, peppers and eggplant indoors in late March.

states.name: Michigan
states.last_frost: early May (southeast) to early June (Upper Peninsula)
states.note: Lake-moderated areas get a longer fall; use it for the cool-season five.

states.name: Minnesota
states.note: Start warm-season crops indoors in April; direct sow cool-season crops as soon as soil can be worked.

states.name: Mississippi
states.note: Plant warm-season crops early and again in late summer for a second harvest.

states.name: Missouri
states.note: Humid heat in July; shade spinach or wait for fall.

states.name: Montana
states.note: Short, cool season; warm-season crops need transplants, black plastic or row cover.

states.name: Nebraska
states.note: Windy; stake tomatoes and peppers well.

states.name: Nevada
states.last_frost: late February (Las Vegas) to late May (Reno and the north)
states.first_frost: late November in the south; late September in the north
states.note: Dry air and alkaline soil; add compost and water consistently.

states.name: New Hampshire
states.note: Start warm-season crops indoors in early April.

states.name: New Jersey
states.note: The Garden State: four full seasons and a long, mild fall for the cool-season five.

states.name: New Mexico
states.last_frost: early April (south) to late May (north and high elevations)
states.first_frost: late October in the south; late September in the north
states.note: Anaheim-type chiles are a home crop here; give peppers full sun.

states.name: New York
states.last_frost: mid-April (New York City and Long Island) to late May (Adirondacks)
states.first_frost: early October upstate to mid-November in the city
states.note: City balconies and rooftops warm up early; start tomatoes indoors in mid-March.

states.name: North Carolina
states.note: Fall is the easiest season for spinach, kale, carrots and beets.

states.name: North Dakota
states.note: Very short season; transplants and row cover for every warm-season crop.

states.name: Ohio
states.note: Reliable four-season garden; two sowings of each cool-season crop.

states.name: Oklahoma
states.note: Hot summers; sow spinach and kale in September for the best harvest.

states.name: Oregon
states.last_frost: mid-April (Willamette Valley) to early June (high desert)
states.first_frost: late October west of the Cascades; late September east
states.note: Cool, wet springs; wait for warm soil before sowing cucumbers and melons.

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.note: Burpee country; tomatoes and peppers do well with a May transplant.

states.name: Rhode Island
states.note: Ocean-moderated; a long fall for the cool-season five.

states.name: South Carolina
states.note: Two warm seasons; plant tomatoes in March and again in July.

states.name: South Dakota
states.note: Short season; choose the warmest, most sheltered spot for melons.

states.name: Tennessee
states.note: Long season with a true second cool season in fall.

states.name: Texas
states.first_frost: early December on the coast; late October in the Panhandle
states.note: Beat the heat: plant tomatoes early, and grow the cool-season five from October through March.

states.name: Utah
states.last_frost: late April (St. George) to late May (Salt Lake and north)
states.note: Dry climate with cold nights; mulch and water deeply.

states.name: Vermont
states.note: Short season; start warm-season crops indoors in early April.

states.name: Virginia
states.note: A long fall makes kale, spinach, carrots and beets easy.

states.name: Washington
states.last_frost: early April (Puget Sound) to late May (eastern Washington)
states.first_frost: late October to mid-November west; early October east
states.note: Cool west-side summers favor the cool-season five; east-side heat suits tomatoes and melons.

states.name: West Virginia
states.last_frost: late April to late May depending on elevation
states.note: Mountain valleys frost late; plant by elevation, not by calendar.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.note: Start warm-season crops indoors in April; sow the cool-season five as soon as the soil thaws.

states.name: Wyoming
states.note: One of the shortest seasons in the country; transplants, row cover and the warmest wall you have.
